course.title: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them
course.lead: A free, self-paced course on every major system in a car: what each part does, how the parts fit together, how to tell when something’s wrong, what you can safely do yourself, and when to stop and call a professional.
how: Start with Lesson 1 for the big picture, then go in order or jump to the system you’re curious about.
Each lesson has diagrams, a “parts and what they do” table, a short quiz and links to go deeper. Badges show the level.
Play with the interactive pieces: the running engine, the brake hydraulics, the differential, the cooling system and more.
Use the troubleshooting finder when something seems wrong, and climb the skill ladder one rung at a time.
course.who: Written for teens and adults with no car experience. It picks up where the car guides in Being an Adult 101 leave off.
course.why: Each lesson explains the “why” as well as the “what”: the physics of a hydraulic brake, the chemistry of a catalytic converter, the math of gears. Facts and numbers come from U.S. government agencies, university automotive and engineering programs, OpenStax textbooks and ASE, and every lesson lists its sources.
course.final: Your owner’s manual is the final word. This course explains how cars work in general. Your owner’s manual and your vehicle’s service information give the exact fluids, pressures, intervals and procedures for your car, and they come first.

lessons.title: The Big Picture
lessons.short: How a car turns fuel or electricity into motion, and a map of every system.
lessons.intro: A car is a team of systems with one job: turn stored energy into motion you can steer and stop. This lesson gives you the map. Every later lesson zooms in on one part of it.

blocks.h: From stored energy to a moving car
blocks.html:
A gasoline car carries its energy as fuel. A pump sends fuel from the tank to the engine, where it’s mixed with air and burned. The hot gases push pistons, the pistons turn a crankshaft, and the transmission carries that turning motion to the wheels. A diesel works the same way, except the fuel lights from the heat of squeezed air instead of a spark.

An electric car carries its energy in a large traction battery. Power electronics feed the battery’s electricity to a motor, and the motor turns the wheels through a transmission. There’s no fuel tank, fuel pump or tailpipe. A hybrid uses both an engine and one or more electric motors.

Whatever the energy source, the last step is the same: the tires push backward on the road, and the road pushes the car forward. That’s Newton’s third law at work, and it’s why the small patches of rubber touching the ground matter so much.

blocks.html:
Burning fuel makes heat, and a heat engine can’t turn all of its heat into work. Some heat always has to flow out to cooler surroundings, which is why an engine needs a radiator and a tailpipe. Physicists write the engine’s efficiency as the useful work out divided by the heat put in.

In combined city and highway driving, only about 16 to 25 percent of the energy in a gasoline car’s fuel ends up moving the car. Engine losses, mostly heat, take 68 to 72 percent. Electric cars waste far less: counting the energy they win back while braking, they deliver about 87 to 91 percent of the energy drawn from the grid to the wheels.

blocks.h: How the systems depend on each other
blocks.html:
No system works alone. The engine needs the electrical system to start it, the fuel system to feed it, the cooling system to keep it from overheating, and oil to keep its parts from grinding together. The engine computer watches all of them through sensors. The brakes, steering, suspension and tires decide what all that power actually does on the road.

That’s why a problem in one system often shows up in another. A weak battery means the engine won’t crank. A thermostat that’s stuck closed makes the engine overheat. A low tire can make the car pull to one side, which feels like a steering problem. When you troubleshoot (Lesson 13), you’ll trace symptoms back across this map.

quiz.q: In combined driving, about how much of a gasoline car’s fuel energy actually moves the car?
quiz.why: About 16 to 25 percent. Most of the rest is lost as engine heat (68 to 72 percent).

quiz.q: Which part turns the pistons’ up-and-down motion into spinning?
quiz.why: The crankshaft. Each piston pushes on it through a connecting rod, like your legs on bicycle pedals.

quiz.q: In an all-electric car, what controls the motor’s speed and torque?
quiz.why: The power electronics controller manages the flow of energy from the traction battery to the motor.

quiz.q: A car won’t crank, and the problem turns out to be the battery. Which system is that?
quiz.why: The battery belongs to the electrical system, which also has to work for the engine to start.

lessons.title: The Engine
lessons.short: The four-stroke cycle and every main part, plus displacement, compression, horsepower and torque.
lessons.intro: An engine is an air pump that powers itself. It pulls in air and fuel, squeezes them, burns them, and pushes out what’s left, over and over, many times every second. Watch it happen, then meet each part.

blocks.cap: Press play, or drag the slider to turn the crank by hand. Tap any part to name it. The valve timing follows typical figures from MIT’s engine course: the intake valve opens a little before the top of the stroke and closes 30 to 50 degrees after the bottom.

blocks.html:
1. Intake. The intake valve opens and the piston moves down, drawing air and fuel into the cylinder.
  2. Compression. Both valves close and the piston moves up, squeezing the mixture into a small space at the top.
  3. Power. The spark plug fires. The burning mixture gets very hot, its pressure soars, and it shoves the piston down. This is the only stroke that makes power.
  4. Exhaust. The exhaust valve opens and the piston moves up, pushing the burned gases out.

Four strokes take two full turns of the crankshaft. Each valve opens once per cycle, so the camshaft that opens the valves turns at half the crankshaft’s speed. Its gear or sprocket is twice the size of the one on the crankshaft, and a timing belt or chain links them.

Real engines don’t open and close the valves exactly at the top and bottom of each stroke. The exhaust valve opens 30 to 50 degrees before the power stroke ends so pressure can blow the gases out, and the intake valve stays open 30 to 50 degrees past the bottom so moving air keeps ramming in. For a moment near the top of the exhaust stroke, both valves are open at once. That’s called valve overlap.

blocks.h: The parts and how they fit
blocks.html: The engine block is the frame. Bored into it are the cylinders, and in each one a piston slides up and down. Piston rings seal the gap between piston and cylinder wall. A connecting rod links each piston to the crankshaft, which runs along the bottom of the block. On top sits the cylinder head, with the valves, the spark plugs and usually the camshafts. The head gasket seals the joint between head and block, and the oil pan closes off the bottom.

blocks.html:
Displacement is the volume all the pistons sweep through in one stroke: the area of the bore times the length of the stroke, times the number of cylinders. It’s a rough measure of how much air an engine can breathe, and it’s usually given in liters. One liter is about 61 cubic inches.

The compression ratio compares the cylinder’s volume with the piston at the bottom to its volume with the piston at the top. Squeezing the mixture harder gets more work out of each drop of fuel, but in a gasoline engine too much squeeze makes the fuel explode on its own, a problem called knock. Knock holds gasoline engines to about 12:1, or about 13:1 with direct injection. Diesels need high compression to light their fuel at all, and run about 14:1 to 22:1; the Navy’s mechanic course lists passenger-car diesels as high as 24:1.

At highway speed, a piston takes combustion pressures over 1,000 psi and temperatures well over 600°F, and it stops and reverses direction about 80 times a second. Engine parts are made with tight tolerances for that reason: a good cylinder is round to within about 0.0005 inch (0.012 mm).

Torque is twisting force: how hard the crankshaft turns. Power is how fast that twisting does work. A rotating shaft’s power is its torque times its rotational speed, so an engine can make big power by twisting hard, by spinning fast, or both.

In U.S. units, one horsepower is 550 foot-pounds of work each second. Working that through gives a handy rule: horsepower equals torque in pound-feet times rpm, divided by 5,252. An engine making 200 pound-feet at 3,000 rpm is making about 114 horsepower. Torque is what you feel pulling away from a stop; power is what keeps the car moving fast. Gears in the transmission trade one for the other (Lesson 7).

power = torque × angular speed  (P = τω)
horsepower = torque (lb·ft) × rpm ÷ 5,252
1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s ≈ 745.7 watts

• Oil level. The simplest engine check there is. See Check Your Engine Oil.
  • Ping. A high-pitched metallic tapping that rises with engine speed is usually fuel with a lower octane rating than the car needs.
  • Heavy knock. A rhythmic pounding can mean worn crankshaft or connecting rod bearings. Stop and have it checked.
  • Blue smoke. Oil is getting into the cylinders and burning, often from worn rings or valve guides.

Technicians measure an engine’s health with tests. A compression test, for example, reads the pressure each cylinder builds while cranking. The Navy’s training manual gives typical readings of about 125 to 175 psi for gasoline engines and 275 to 400 psi for diesels; your engine’s service information has the real numbers, and evenness between cylinders matters as much as the figure itself.

Anything inside the engine, such as timing belts and chains, head gaskets, valves and bearings, takes special tools, exact specifications and the service information for your engine. Leave it to a trained technician, and stop driving if you hear a heavy knock or the oil pressure light comes on.

lessons.title: Air, Fuel and Spark
lessons.short: Intake, sensors, fuel delivery, ignition and the engine computer’s closed loop; how diesels differ.
lessons.intro: A gasoline engine needs three things at once: the right amount of air, the right amount of fuel for that air, and a spark at the right instant. A computer juggles all three, adjusting them constantly as you drive.

blocks.html:
Gasoline burns completely with about 14.7 pounds of air for every pound of fuel. That’s the chemically correct, or stoichiometric, mix. A mix with extra fuel is called rich; one with extra air is lean. Because the chemistry depends on how many molecules of air there are, the engine computer cares about the air’s mass, not just its volume.

In a gasoline engine you control power with air. The throttle is a valve in the intake: press the pedal and it opens, more air flows in, and the computer adds fuel to match. A diesel works the other way around, as you’ll see below.

Air enters through the air filter, which keeps sand, dust and lint out of the engine. Dirt that gets in causes engine wear and poor combustion. Next, an airflow sensor measures the air. A common type has a heated platinum wire in the air stream: the more air rushing past, the more power it takes to keep the wire hot, and that tells the computer how much air is coming in. The air then passes the throttle and the intake manifold, which splits it among the cylinders.

Late-model cars use an electric fuel pump, usually inside the tank. It pushes fuel through the lines and a filter to the fuel injectors. A pressure regulator holds the fuel at a set pressure. Some vehicles also have an inertia switch that shuts the pump off in a crash or rollover.

An injector is an electrically controlled valve. When the computer energizes its solenoid, the nozzle opens and sprays fuel; a spring snaps it shut. The computer sets the amount of fuel by changing how long each injector stays open. Some engines spray into the intake ports, others straight into the combustion chamber (direct injection).

A spark plug needs roughly 4,000 to 10,000 volts to jump its gap. The ignition coil turns the car’s 12 volts into 30,000 volts or more, plenty to fire the plug every time.

Timing matters as much as voltage. Normal combustion takes about three thousandths of a second, so the plug fires before the piston reaches the top. The goal is peak pressure just after top dead center, about 14 to 17 degrees of crank rotation past it in a typical gasoline engine, when the piston can use the push best.

The electronic control module (ECM), the engine computer, manages the fuel mixture, ignition timing and emissions controls. It also watches over the engine, protects it, and records problems it finds.

Its most important helper is the oxygen sensor in the exhaust. A common type is a small ceramic cell that makes a voltage: high when the exhaust is rich (little leftover oxygen), low when it’s lean. The computer reads that signal and trims the injector open time, then checks the result and trims again. That feedback is called closed-loop control. A cold sensor doesn’t work well, so most have a built-in heater; until they’re ready, the computer runs on preset values (open loop).

blocks.html:
A diesel draws in air only and squeezes it hard, which makes it very hot. Then it sprays fuel into that hot air at a measured rate, and the fuel lights on contact. There are no spark plugs. Some diesels have glow plugs that heat the air in a small chamber to help cold starts. A diesel controls its speed with the amount of fuel injected, not by throttling the air.

A turbocharger is a fan spun by the exhaust that forces more air into the engine under pressure. It can turn up to 100,000 rpm, so engine oil lubricates its shaft bearings. Modern diesels also clean their exhaust: a particulate filter traps soot, an oxidation catalyst cleans other pollutants, and diesel exhaust fluid (a urea and water solution kept in its own tank) is sprayed in so a selective catalytic reduction unit can turn nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and water.

• Check and replace the engine air filter at the interval your owner’s manual lists. On most cars it sits in a box you can open by hand or with a screwdriver.
  • Use the fuel your manual or fuel door specifies, including the octane rating.
  • Make sure the gas cap clicks tight. A loose cap can turn on the check engine light (Lesson 5).

Gasoline vapor catches fire easily. If you smell raw fuel strongly, or see fuel dripping, don’t start the car; have it checked. A flashing check engine light usually means a serious misfire: get it looked at right away and drive as little as possible.

quiz.q: About how many pounds of air does a gasoline engine need to burn one pound of fuel completely?
quiz.why: About 14.7 pounds of air per pound of fuel. That’s the stoichiometric ratio.

quiz.q: What does the oxygen sensor tell the engine computer?
opts: Whether the exhaust is rich or lean
How fast the car is going
quiz.why: It reports rich (high voltage) or lean (low voltage), and the computer corrects the fuel.

quiz.q: How does the engine computer change the amount of fuel injected?
opts: By changing the fuel pump speed only
By changing how long the injector stays open
By changing the spark plug gap
quiz.why: It varies how long each injector nozzle stays open.

quiz.q: What lights the fuel in a diesel engine?
opts: The heat of the squeezed air
quiz.why: Diesels use compression ignition: air is squeezed until it’s hot enough to light the fuel sprayed into it.

lessons.title: Cooling and Lubrication
lessons.short: Radiator, water pump, thermostat, coolant and heater core; oil pump, filter, passages and pressure.
lessons.intro: Most of the energy in fuel turns into heat, and an engine full of hot, fast-moving metal needs two things to survive: a way to shed that heat, and a film of oil between every moving part.

blocks.html:
In Lesson 1 you saw that engine losses, mostly heat, eat 68 to 72 percent of a gasoline car’s fuel energy. Some leaves with the exhaust; the cylinder walls, head and pistons soak up the rest. Without a cooling system they would get hot enough to break down the oil film and damage the metal.

An engine also shouldn’t run too cold. It’s designed to warm up quickly and work best at its normal operating temperature, which is why the cooling system has a thermostat.

The water pump pushes coolant through passages in the block and head called the water jacket, where it picks up heat. The hot coolant flows out through the upper hose to the radiator. There it spreads into many small tubes with thin fins, and air flowing through carries the heat away. At speed, the car’s motion pushes air through; when it’s moving slowly or stopped, the fan pulls air through instead. The cooled liquid returns through the lower hose to the pump.

The thermostat is a valve between the engine and the radiator. When the engine is cold it stays closed, keeping heat in the engine so it warms up fast. As the engine reaches operating temperature it opens and adjusts the flow to the radiator to hold a steady temperature.

Your heater runs on the same loop. Hot coolant passes through the heater core, a small radiator behind the dashboard, and a blower pushes cabin air across it.

blocks.cap: A simplified model with a temperature gauge instead of degrees, since normal operating temperatures vary by engine. Try each scenario to see how a failed part shows up on the gauge.

blocks.html:
The radiator cap has two spring-loaded valves. The pressure valve lets the system build a little pressure, and pressure raises the coolant’s boiling point, the same physics as a pressure cooker. The vacuum valve opens as the engine cools so coolant can flow back from the overflow reservoir instead of the hoses collapsing.

That pressure is also why you never open a hot cooling system. Steam and boiling coolant can spray out and burn you. Check the coolant level at the see-through reservoir, with the engine cold.

Coolant is a mix of water and antifreeze, usually ethylene glycol, plus corrosion inhibitors. Water alone would freeze in winter, and since water expands about 9 percent when it freezes, it could crack the engine. A half-and-half mix of ethylene glycol and water protects to about −34°F. Use the type and mix your owner’s manual specifies.

Ethylene glycol tastes sweet and is poisonous to swallow. Keep antifreeze bottles closed, off the ground, and out of the reach of children.

Engine oil does more than make things slippery. It reduces friction between moving parts, cushions them with a film so metal doesn’t touch metal, carries away heat, helps seal the piston rings against the cylinder walls, carries dirt to the filter, and coats parts so they don’t corrode. Oil’s resistance to flow is its viscosity. It thins as it heats, so it has to be thin enough to flow when cold and thick enough to hold a film when hot.

In a car engine, oil is pumped under pressure. It sits in the oil pan. An engine-driven pump draws it up through a screen and pushes it through the oil filter into drilled passages, the oil galleries, that lead to the crankshaft and camshaft bearings and the valve train. A relief valve keeps the pressure from climbing too high, and a bypass valve lets oil around a clogged filter so the engine still gets some. The oil then drains back to the pan and the cycle repeats.

  • Change your own oil and filter once you’ve done it with help (Change Your Own Oil and Filter). Take the used oil to a collection site: the used oil from one oil change can contaminate a million gallons of fresh water.

  • Never remove the radiator cap or open any part of the pressurized system until it has cooled.
  • If the red oil pressure light comes on while driving, pull over when it’s safe and shut the engine off. Check the oil level once it has settled, and have the car checked before you drive it far. Your owner’s manual describes this light for your car.

quiz.q: A cold engine’s thermostat is closed. Why?
opts: So the engine warms up quickly
quiz.why: Keeping coolant out of the radiator holds heat in the engine so it reaches operating temperature fast.

quiz.q: Why does the cooling system run under pressure?
opts: Pressure raises the coolant’s boiling point
It makes the pump spin faster
It keeps air out of the tires
quiz.why: Higher pressure means a higher boiling point, so the coolant can run hotter without boiling.

quiz.q: A car overheats in stop-and-go traffic but is fine on the highway. Which part is a likely suspect?
quiz.why: At highway speed, air rushes through the radiator by itself. In traffic, the fan has to do that job.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of oil’s jobs?
quiz.why: Oil lubricates, cushions, cools, seals, cleans and protects against corrosion. The radiator cap’s pressure raises the coolant’s boiling point.

quiz.q: What does the oil pressure relief valve do?
opts: Keeps oil pressure from climbing too high
quiz.why: It opens when pressure gets too high and sends extra oil back.

lessons.title: Exhaust and Emissions
lessons.short: Manifold, catalytic converter, oxygen sensors, muffler, EGR, EVAP, OBD-II and reading codes.
lessons.intro: Burned gases leave the engine hot, loud and full of pollutants. The exhaust system carries them out, quiets them, and cleans them up, while the engine computer watches every step and tells you when something goes wrong.

blocks.html: Exhaust leaves each cylinder through the exhaust manifold, which gathers it into one pipe. It flows past an oxygen sensor, through the catalytic converter, past a second oxygen sensor, through the muffler, and out the tailpipe. The upstream sensor helps the computer set the fuel mixture; the downstream one lets it check whether the converter is still doing its job.

blocks.html:
Inside the converter, the exhaust flows over surfaces coated with catalytic metals, most often platinum and rhodium. A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. In a modern three-way converter, carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons combine with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water vapor, and nitrogen oxides are split back into nitrogen and oxygen. These reactions work best when the engine runs close to the chemically correct air-fuel ratio, which is one reason the computer works so hard to hold it there.

The first catalytic converters arrived in 1975. Unleaded gasoline was introduced at the same time, because lead in gasoline ruins converters.

blocks.h: Three loops that keep pollution in
blocks.html:
• EGR (exhaust gas recirculation) sends a little exhaust back into the intake. Exhaust won’t burn again, so it soaks up heat and lowers the peak combustion temperature, and cooler burning makes less nitrogen oxide.
  • PCV (positive crankcase ventilation) handles blow-by: combustion gases that sneak past the piston rings into the crankcase. Instead of venting them to the air, the PCV system draws them into the intake to be burned.
  • EVAP (evaporative emissions) catches gasoline vapor from the tank in a canister of activated charcoal. When the engine runs, the canister is purged and the vapor is burned. That’s why a loose or missing gas cap can turn on the check engine light: the system tests itself for leaks.

Every car and light truck from the 1996 model year on has a second-generation on-board diagnostic system, OBD-II. It monitors emission-related parts for wear and failure. When it finds a problem, it stores a diagnostic trouble code and turns on the check engine light, which is usually yellow.

  • Steady light: the car may not be running properly. It isn’t an emergency, but get it diagnosed soon. First, check that the gas cap is tight; after a loose cap is fixed, the light should go off within a few days.
  • Flashing light: a severe misfire is happening. Unburned fuel can overheat and seriously damage the catalytic converter, often the most expensive part to replace. Get it addressed right away, drive as little as possible, and avoid high speeds and heavy loads.

blocks.h: Reading codes with a scan tool
blocks.html: The standard diagnostic connector sits under the dashboard on the driver’s side. A scan tool plugs in and reads the stored codes. Codes that start with P are powertrain codes (engine and transmission); C, B and U codes cover chassis, body and network problems. In a P code, a second digit of 0 marks a standard code that means the same on every car, and 1 marks a manufacturer’s own code. The third digit names the area: for example, 3 means the ignition system or a misfire.

blocks.cap: Type a code to see what each part means. The common codes listed come from New Jersey’s emissions inspection program.

blocks.h: A code is a clue, not a diagnosis
blocks.html:
A misfire code such as P0301 tells you the engine is misfiring, not why. The cause could be a spark plug, an ignition coil, an injector or a compression problem. Good technicians test before they replace parts.

Clearing codes doesn’t fix anything. It also resets the car’s readiness monitors, the self-tests an emissions inspection checks, and a car can fail inspection as “not ready” until it has been driven enough for them to run again; most cars get there in a few minutes of normal driving, but some need several days of mixed city and highway driving.

Federal rules require emission warranties: for 1995 and newer cars, the on-board computer and the catalytic converter are covered for 8 years or 80,000 miles. Check before you pay for those repairs.

blocks.html: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, an odorless, colorless gas that kills without warning. A small leak in the exhaust system can let it build up inside the car, so the CDC advises having a mechanic check the exhaust system every year. Never run a car or truck inside a garage attached to a house, even with the garage door open. A rotten-egg smell usually points to the catalytic converter or another emission control part.

lessons.title: The Electrical System
lessons.short: Battery, alternator, starter, fuses and relays, grounds, reading simple wiring, safe multimeter checks.
lessons.intro: Every modern car runs on electricity, even one that burns gasoline. The battery starts the engine, the alternator keeps everything powered once it’s running, and a web of wires, fuses and grounds carries current to every light, sensor and computer.

blocks.html: Voltage is electrical pressure: the push that makes charge move. Current, measured in amperes (amps), is how much charge flows. Resistance, measured in ohms, is how hard the path is to push through. Ohm’s law ties them together. For example, a 12-volt battery pushing through 6 ohms drives 2 amps; through 8 ohms, only 1.5 amps.
voltage = current × resistance  <small>(E = I × R, so I = E ÷ R)</small>

A car battery is a lead-acid battery: plates of lead and lead dioxide in sulfuric acid. Each cell makes about 2 volts, so six cells in series make a 12-volt battery. It’s rechargeable: running current backward through it reverses the chemical reaction.

A well-charged 12-volt battery reads a bit over 12 volts with the engine off. The Navy’s mechanic course says a reading around 11.5 volts means it’s undercharged or may be bad. Charging a battery gives off hydrogen gas, which can explode if a spark or flame reaches it, so batteries are charged in a ventilated space, away from sparks and smoking.

When you turn the key or press the start button, a small current flows through the ignition switch to the starter solenoid. The solenoid is a heavy-duty switch: it connects the battery to the starter motor with a big current, and the starter spins the engine’s flywheel until the engine runs on its own. On automatic transmissions, a neutral safety switch lets the starter work only in Park or Neutral. Don’t crank the engine for more than 30 seconds at a time, or the starter can be damaged.

Once the engine runs, a belt spins the alternator, a generator. Spinning a magnetic field past coils of wire makes alternating current. Six diodes in a rectifier turn that into direct current for the battery and the car. A voltage regulator controls the output; most hold about 13.5 to 14.5 volts. That’s why a healthy charging system reads higher with the engine running than the battery does with it off.

blocks.html:
Electricity needs a complete loop. Cars save a wire in nearly every circuit by using the steel body and frame as the return path: one battery terminal, the negative on most cars, is connected to the body, and each part is grounded to the metal near it. A loose or corroded ground breaks the loop just as surely as a cut wire.

  • Open circuit: a break in the path, such as a loose wire, a corroded terminal or a blown fuse. Nothing works.
  • Short circuit: current takes a shortcut, often where insulation has worn through. Too much current flows and can overheat the wiring and start a fire.
  • Fuses protect against shorts: a thin metal strip melts and opens the circuit before the wiring overheats.
  • Relays let a small current control a big one. Current through a small coil makes a magnetic field that pulls a switch closed, the same idea as the starter solenoid.

Parts can be wired in series, one after another, so a single break stops everything, or in parallel, side by side, so one failure doesn’t affect the others. That’s why one burned-out headlight doesn’t turn off the other.

Trace a circuit the way current flows: from the battery’s positive side, through the fuse, through the switch, to the load (a lamp, motor or other device), and then to ground. When a load doesn’t work, a technician checks each link in that chain: power at the fuse, power through the switch, power at the load, and a good ground.

blocks.html:
A digital multimeter set to DC volts is a safe first tool. Touch the red probe to the battery’s positive terminal and the black probe to the negative terminal.

  • Engine off: a well-charged battery reads a bit over 12 volts. Around 11.5 volts means it’s low or failing.
  • Engine running: most charging systems hold about 13.5 to 14.5 volts. A reading close to the engine-off number suggests the alternator isn’t charging.

Check voltage with the meter across two points. Leave current measurements on car circuits to experienced hands: the starter draws far more current than a hand meter can carry. Check a fuse by eye (a broken strip) or by testing continuity with the fuse pulled out of its socket, and replace it only with one of the same amp rating.

blocks.html:
• Measure battery voltage, engine off and running, as above.
  • Find the fuse boxes and fuse chart in your owner’s manual, and replace a blown fuse with one of the same rating.
  • Keep the battery terminals clean and tight. Wear eye protection: battery acid is caustic.
  • Learn to jump-start a car safely: Jump-Start a Car.

A fuse that blows again right away means a short somewhere; find the cause rather than fitting a bigger fuse. A smell like burned toast often signals an electrical short and burning insulation. Wiring repairs, computer problems and anything near the airbag system belong with a technician. In hybrids and electric cars, anything orange or marked high-voltage is off-limits (Lesson 11).

quiz.q: A 12-volt battery drives current through a 6-ohm circuit. How much current flows?

quiz.q: Why does a car battery read more voltage with the engine running?
quiz.why: The alternator and regulator hold the system at about 13.5 to 14.5 volts while the engine runs.

quiz.q: What does a fuse do?
opts: Melts to open the circuit before the wiring overheats
quiz.why: A fuse is a deliberate weak link that protects the wiring.

quiz.q: In most cars, what carries current back to the battery?

lessons.title: Transmission and Drivetrain
lessons.short: Gears and torque, clutch and manual gearbox, automatics, CVTs, driveshafts, differentials and drive layouts.
lessons.intro: An engine makes useful power only within a range of speeds, but a car has to crawl out of a parking space and cruise on the highway. The transmission bridges that gap, and the rest of the drivetrain carries the power to the wheels.

blocks.html:
When a small gear drives a larger one, the larger gear turns more slowly but with more torque. When a large gear drives a smaller one, the output spins faster with less torque. Power, which is torque times rotational speed, stays the same apart from a little friction. Gears don’t create power; they trade speed for twisting force.

Low gears multiply torque to get the car moving. High gears let the engine turn slowly at highway speed. The differential adds one more fixed reduction, the final drive. Passenger cars typically use final drive ratios of about 3:1 to 5:1.

gear ratio = driven gear teeth ÷ driving gear teeth
output torque ≈ input torque × ratio    output speed = input speed ÷ ratio

blocks.cap: Set the gear sizes and engine output to see torque and speed trade places. Then take the car around a turn and watch the differential at work. Starting values are examples, not figures for any particular car.

blocks.html: A manual transmission needs a way to disconnect the engine while you change gears. That’s the clutch: a friction disc pinched between the engine’s flywheel and a spring-loaded pressure plate. Pressing the clutch pedal releases the pressure plate so the disc can slip free. Inside the gearbox, pairs of gears with different sizes give each ratio.

An automatic connects to the engine through a torque converter, a fluid coupling with three main parts. The impeller, turned by the engine, flings transmission fluid outward. The fluid strikes the fins of the turbine, which drives the transmission. Between them, a stator on a one-way clutch redirects the returning fluid; at low speed, when the impeller is turning much faster than the turbine, that adds to the torque reaching the turbine. When you’re stopped at a light, the turbine stands still and the converter simply slips. Once the speeds nearly match, many converters engage a lock-up clutch that ties the engine directly to the transmission, cutting losses at steady speeds.

The gears inside are usually planetary gear sets: a sun gear in the middle, planet gears on a carrier around it, and a ring gear with teeth on the inside. One member drives, one is held still, and the third carries the power out; holding different members gives different ratios, and locking two together gives direct drive. Clutches and bands do the holding, and a transmission control module chooses shifts using shift solenoids, reading sensors such as wheel speed, throttle position and fluid temperature.

A belt-type CVT has no fixed gears. It uses two pulleys whose halves are cone-shaped and can slide closer or farther apart, with a belt or chain between them. Squeezing a pulley’s halves together pushes the belt to a larger radius; spreading them lets it drop lower. One pulley sets the ratio while the other keeps the belt tight, so the ratio changes smoothly. That lets the engine hold its most efficient or most powerful speed while the car speeds up.

On rear-wheel-drive vehicles, a hollow steel driveshaft carries power from the transmission back to the rear axle. Universal joints let it work at an angle as the suspension moves, and a slip yoke lets it change length. Front-drive cars use constant-velocity (CV) joints at each end of the front axles, since the front wheels both steer and drive.

In a turn, the outside wheel travels a bigger circle than the inside wheel, so it has to turn faster. If both wheels were locked to one axle, one tire would have to skid. The differential solves that. The driveshaft’s pinion gear turns a large ring gear, which spins the differential carrier. Inside the carrier, small spider gears drive two side gears, one for each axle. Going straight, the spider gears don’t spin on their shaft and both wheels turn together. In a turn, they turn, letting one side speed up while the other slows by the same amount: the carrier’s speed is always the average of the two wheels.

The catch: an ordinary (open) differential sends the most torque to the wheel with the least traction, so one wheel on ice can spin while the other does nothing. A limited-slip differential sends more torque to the wheel with better grip.

blocks.h: Front, rear, all and four-wheel drive
blocks.html:
Front-wheel-drive cars put the engine and a transaxle, a transmission and differential in one unit, over the front wheels. Rear-wheel drive sends power back through a driveshaft to a rear differential. All-wheel drive powers both axles all the time, with a center differential or similar device so the front and rear can turn at different speeds. Traditional part-time four-wheel drive uses a transfer case to lock the front axle to the rear, often with a low range for extra torque; because it has no center differential, it’s meant for loose or slippery surfaces, and running it engaged on dry pavement can damage the drivetrain. Your owner’s manual explains your system.

All- and four-wheel drive are now common: 59 percent of new light-duty vehicles built in 2022 had one or the other. They improve traction, but the extra parts add weight and friction that can lower fuel economy.

quiz.q: A 12-tooth gear drives a 36-tooth gear. What happens to the output?
opts: Three times the speed, a third the torque
A third the speed, about three times the torque
It turns backward at the same speed
quiz.why: The ratio is 36 ÷ 12 = 3:1. The output turns one-third as fast with about three times the torque.

quiz.q: Why does a car need a differential?
opts: So the wheels can turn at different speeds in a turn
quiz.why: The outside wheel travels farther in a turn; the differential lets it turn faster than the inside wheel.

quiz.q: In a turn, the inside wheel turns at 90 percent and the outside wheel at 110 percent of the carrier speed. What is the carrier’s speed?
quiz.why: The carrier turns at the average of the two wheels: (90 + 110) ÷ 2 = 100 percent.

quiz.q: Which part of a torque converter multiplies torque at low speed?
quiz.why: The stator redirects fluid returning from the turbine, which adds to the torque at the turbine.

quiz.q: Why shouldn’t part-time four-wheel drive stay engaged on dry pavement?
opts: With no center differential, the drivetrain binds in turns and can be damaged
quiz.why: Front and rear axles travel different distances in a turn. Without a center differential, the tires must skip or the parts strain.

lessons.title: Brakes
lessons.short: Hydraulics and Pascal’s principle, master cylinder, lines, calipers, pads, rotors, drums, fluid, ABS and regenerative braking.
lessons.intro: Brakes turn the energy of a moving car into heat. Your foot supplies only a small push; a lever and a hydraulic system multiply it into thousands of pounds of squeeze at the wheels.

blocks.html:
Push on a liquid sealed in a container and the pressure rises the same amount everywhere in it. That’s Pascal’s principle. Pressure is force divided by area, so a small piston and a large piston connected by a line feel the same pressure, and the large one pushes with more force: force out ÷ area out = force in ÷ area in.

There’s no free lunch. The large piston moves a shorter distance, so the work out is no more than the work in. OpenStax’s physics textbook works an example: a 100-newton push on the pedal becomes 500 newtons at the pedal cylinder through a lever. With a pedal cylinder 0.500 cm across and wheel cylinders 2.50 cm across, each wheel cylinder pushes with about 12,500 newtons, 25 times more.
F<sub>out</sub> = F<sub>in</sub> × (A<sub>out</sub> ÷ A<sub>in</sub>)    and since A = π d² ÷ 4, the force grows with the square of the diameter ratio

blocks.cap: Change the push, the lever and the piston sizes. The starting values reproduce the OpenStax example. Real cars add a power booster, so these are physics numbers, not specifications for any car.

blocks.html:
The brake pedal is a lever that pushes a piston in the master cylinder. Modern cars use a dual (tandem) master cylinder with two pistons and two circuits, split front-and-rear or corner-to-corner, so a leak in one circuit leaves the other still working. A warning switch lights the brake light on the dashboard if the pressure in the two circuits gets out of balance.

From the master cylinder, double-walled steel lines carry fluid toward each wheel, with flexible rubber hoses where parts move, such as to the front calipers. A power booster adds force to your push; most use engine vacuum, and a steady hiss when you press the pedal can mean a vacuum leak.

A disc brake has a rotor, a metal disc that turns with the wheel, and a caliper that straddles it. Fluid pressure pushes the caliper’s piston, and the pads squeeze both sides of the rotor. A floating caliper slides sideways on its mounts; a fixed caliper has pistons on both sides. Many pads have a small metal wear indicator that squeals or screeches against the rotor when the pads get thin. Pads and rotors are replaced in pairs, both sides of an axle.

A drum brake has two curved shoes inside a drum that turns with the wheel. A wheel cylinder pushes the shoes outward against the drum. The drum’s rotation tends to drag the leading shoe in tighter, a self-energizing effect that adds to the braking force.

blocks.html: Brake fluid has to stay liquid and resist boiling even when the brakes get very hot, because boiling would make gas bubbles, and gas squeezes where liquid doesn’t. Most fluids (DOT 3, DOT 4 and DOT 5.1) are glycol-based and absorb moisture from the air over time, which lowers their boiling point. That’s why the federal standard requires every container to say: “Keep container clean and tightly closed to prevent absorption of moisture.” DOT 5 is silicone-based and dyed purple. Use only the type printed on your reservoir cap or in your owner’s manual.

blocks.h: ABS, parking brakes and regenerative braking
blocks.html:
A locked, skidding wheel can’t steer. Antilock brakes (ABS) watch each wheel with a speed sensor. When a wheel starts to lock, the ABS computer opens a valve to release that wheel’s pressure for an instant, then reapplies it, keeping the tire just short of skidding, where grip is greatest and you can still steer.

The parking brake is a separate, mechanical way to hold the car, on many cars a cable to the rear brakes. Hybrids and electric cars also brake regeneratively: the motor runs as a generator, turning motion back into electricity for the battery. That captures energy normally lost as heat and significantly reduces brake wear, but the friction brakes are still there for hard stops.

  • Listen for squealing from the wear indicators and look at the pads through the wheel if you can see them.
  • Never blow brake dust away with compressed air, and don’t clean brakes with a dry rag or brush. Some brake parts may contain asbestos, and you can’t tell by looking. EPA suggests home mechanics use a wet-wipe method: mist the parts with water, then wipe them clean.

Have the brakes checked before you drive further if the pedal feels spongy, sinks toward the floor when you hold it, or feels much harder than usual; if you hear or feel scraping or grinding; if the car pulls to one side when you brake; or if the red brake light stays on. A spongy pedal usually means air in the lines; a sinking pedal can mean a leak inside the master cylinder.

quiz.q: What does Pascal’s principle say?
opts: Pressure in a sealed liquid changes the same amount everywhere
Heat flows from cold to hot
quiz.why: A change in pressure on an enclosed fluid is passed on undiminished to every part of it.

quiz.q: A caliper piston has twice the diameter of the master cylinder piston. How much more force does it push with?
quiz.why: Area grows with the square of diameter: 2² = 4 times the area, so 4 times the force at the same pressure.

quiz.q: Why do most brake fluids need replacing over time?
opts: They absorb moisture, which lowers the boiling point
They turn into gas when cold
quiz.why: Glycol fluids absorb water from the air, and the wet boiling points are much lower than the dry ones.

quiz.q: Why do cars have two brake circuits?
opts: So a leak in one still leaves some braking
quiz.why: The dual master cylinder keeps one circuit working if the other fails.

quiz.q: What does ABS prevent?
quiz.why: By releasing and reapplying pressure, ABS keeps the wheels turning so you can still steer.

lessons.title: Steering, Suspension and Alignment
lessons.short: Rack and pinion, power steering, springs, shocks and struts, control arms, ball joints, tie rods, sway bars, camber, caster and toe.
lessons.intro: The suspension keeps the tires pressed to the road while the body rides smoothly over bumps, and the steering points the front wheels where you want to go. Alignment is the set of small angles that makes it all track straight.

blocks.html:
Springs hold the car up and let the wheels move over bumps without lifting the body. Most cars use coil springs; trucks often use leaf springs, stacked strips of spring steel, and some vehicles use torsion bars, steel rods that twist.

A spring alone would keep bouncing after every bump. A shock absorber stops that: as the wheel moves, a piston forces hydraulic fluid through small openings, which slows the motion and turns the bouncing energy into heat. Coil springs have almost no friction of their own, so they always need shocks. Worn shocks or other suspension parts make the ride bouncy and cornering poor.

Control arms hold the wheel’s steering knuckle and let it move up and down; rubber bushings at their inner ends act as bearings. Ball joints at the outer ends are swivels that let the knuckle move up and down and turn for steering. Many cars use a MacPherson strut, which combines the shock absorber and coil spring in one unit, so only a lower control arm and the strut hold the front wheel. A stabilizer bar, or sway bar, links the two sides and twists to limit body roll in turns.

blocks.html:
Many cars use rack-and-pinion steering. A small pinion gear on the end of the steering shaft meshes with a long toothed bar, the rack. Turning the wheel slides the rack side to side, and tie rods at its ends push and pull the steering arms on the knuckles. The gearing multiplies your effort: in one example from the Navy’s mechanic course, 10 pounds on the steering wheel can produce up to 270 pounds at the wheels.

Power steering adds more help. Hydraulic systems use an engine-driven pump, and their pressure can exceed 1,000 psi. Electric power steering uses a motor and a torque sensor instead, and the motor works only when you’re steering, which saves energy. It also drops the pump, hoses, fluid and drive belt.

• Camber is the tilt of the wheel seen from the front: top out is positive, top in is negative. Incorrect camber wears the tire smoothly on one side, and the car leads toward the side with more camber.
  • Caster is the tilt of the steering axis seen from the side; top tilted back is positive. Positive caster helps the steering return to center and keeps the car stable, like the wheels of a shopping cart trailing behind their pivots. Uneven caster makes the car lead toward the side with less.
  • Toe is whether the fronts of the tires point toward each other (toe-in) or away (toe-out), seen from above. Toe is the biggest tire-wearing angle; wrong toe scuffs the tread into feathered, saw-tooth edges.

Setting alignment takes special equipment and a qualified technician. A car that pulls to one side on a straight, level road may need it, but check the simple thing first: an under-inflated tire can cause a pull too.

Sagging; a technician checks ride height.

blocks.html:
• Keep the tires at the recommended pressure; low tires cause hard steering and pulling (Check Tire Pressure and Tread).
  • Watch your tires for uneven wear, which often points to alignment or worn parts (Lesson 10).
  • Notice changes: new clunks, a crooked steering wheel when driving straight, or the car drifting.

Suspension and steering parts hold the car on the road, and springs store a lot of energy. Replacing them, and setting alignment, are jobs for a technician with the right tools and specifications. Get the car checked promptly if steering suddenly gets loose or heavy, or if you hear a new clunk from the front end.

quiz.q: What does a shock absorber do?
opts: Damps bouncing by forcing fluid through small openings
quiz.why: Springs hold the car up; shocks slow the springs’ motion so the car doesn’t keep bouncing.

quiz.q: Which alignment angle wears tires fastest when it’s wrong?
quiz.why: Toe is called the biggest tire-wearing angle; it scrubs the tires sideways as they roll.

quiz.q: What helps the steering wheel return to center after a turn?
quiz.why: With the steering axis tilted back, the tire trails behind its pivot like a shopping-cart wheel and pulls itself straight.

quiz.q: A car drifts to the right on a level road. What should you check first?
quiz.why: Under-inflated tires can cause pulling; check them before paying for an alignment.

lessons.title: Wheels and Tires in Depth
lessons.short: The sidewall code, load index and speed rating, TPMS, wear patterns and what they mean, rotation and balancing.
lessons.intro: Everything the car does, it does through four small patches of rubber. Reading a tire’s sidewall and its tread tells you a great deal about the tire and about the rest of the car.

blocks.html: Take the size P215/65R15 95H. The P means a passenger-vehicle tire. 215 is the width in millimeters from sidewall to sidewall. 65 is the aspect ratio: the sidewall’s height is 65 percent of the width. R means radial construction, which gives a flexible sidewall and a stiff tread. 15 is the wheel diameter in inches. 95 is the load index, a code for how much weight the tire can carry, and H is the speed symbol.

blocks.cap: Type a size from your own tire, or try LT245/75R16. The sizes and diameter are worked out from the code itself.
Speed symbols (NHTSA)
head: Symbol
Maximum speed

blocks.html:
• Load index is a code number, not pounds; tire charts turn it into a weight. Your owner’s manual or a tire dealer can tell you what your car needs.
  • Maximum permissible inflation pressure is the most the tire should ever hold. It is not your car’s recommended pressure.
  • Tire Identification Number: the letters DOT, then the plant code and more. The last four digits are the week and year it was made: 0308 means the third week of 2008. It may be printed on only one side.
  • Treadwear, traction and temperature grades (UTQG): a treadwear grade of 200 should last about twice as long as 100 under the same test; traction runs AA, A, B, C for stopping on wet pavement; temperature runs A, B, C for resisting heat.

The right pressure for your tires is the one the vehicle maker lists on the tire and loading information label, on the driver’s door edge or door post, or in the owner’s manual. Check all the tires, including the spare, at least once a month and before long trips, when they’re cold, meaning parked for at least three hours. Pressure changes about 1 psi for every 10°F change in temperature, so tires read low on the first cold morning of fall.

Cars from the 2008 model year on have a tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS), which lights a warning when a tire is significantly under-inflated. It isn’t a substitute for a gauge: by the time it lights, the tire is already well below where it should be. If the TPMS light flashes for 60 to 90 seconds and then stays on, the system itself may have a problem. The step-by-step check is in Check Tire Pressure and Tread.

Tires should be replaced when the tread is worn to 2/32 inch. Built-in wear bars in the grooves show when you’ve reached it, and the penny test works too: put a penny head-first into a groove; if you can see the top of Lincoln’s head, it’s time. Tires also age. You can’t see aging just by looking, and some vehicle and tire makers recommend replacing tires 6 to 10 years old regardless of tread.

blocks.h: Wear patterns and what they mean
blocks.html:
• Center worn, edges fine: too much air; the tire bulges in the middle.
  • Both edges worn: too little air; the sides sag and carry the load.
  • One edge worn: the wheels are out of alignment (often camber).
  • Feathered, saw-tooth edges: toe is off.
  • Random patchy spots: wheels out of balance, or worn shocks or ball joints.

blocks.html: Rotating the tires, moving them front to back and side to side, evens out wear. If your manufacturer recommends it, the usual interval is every 5,000 to 8,000 miles, or sooner if you see uneven wear; some vehicles, such as those with different front and rear sizes, can’t be rotated. Balancing adds small weights to the wheel to cancel heavy spots so the wheel doesn’t shake; new tires should always be balanced when installed. Alignment sets the wheel angles (Lesson 9).

blocks.html:
• Check pressure monthly with your own gauge, and keep the gauge in the car.
  • Check tread with the wear bars or the penny test, and look for cuts, bulges and uneven wear.
  • Learn to change a flat: Change a Flat Tire. A spare isn’t a replacement for worn tires.

Don’t drive on a tire with a bulge, a cut into the cords, or a sidewall puncture; sidewall punctures shouldn’t be repaired. Under-inflated and overloaded tires are a major cause of tire failure. Mounting and balancing need a tire shop’s machines.

opts: The sidewall height is 65 percent of the width
quiz.why: 65 is the aspect ratio: sidewall height as a percentage of the tire’s width.

quiz.q: Where do you find the right pressure for your tires?
opts: The maximum printed on the sidewall
The label on the driver’s door edge or post, or the owner’s manual
quiz.why: Use the vehicle maker’s figure. The sidewall number is the maximum the tire can hold, not the target.

quiz.q: A tire is worn in the center but fine at the edges. What’s the likely cause?
quiz.why: Too much air makes the tire bulge in the middle, so the center wears first.

quiz.q: A tire’s DOT code ends in 4521. When was it made?
quiz.why: The last four digits are week and year: week 45 of 2021.

quiz.q: Your TPMS light comes on. What does it tell you?
opts: At least one tire is significantly under-inflated
quiz.why: TPMS warns only when a tire is well below the right pressure. Check all four with a gauge.

lessons.title: Hybrids and Electric Cars
lessons.short: Battery pack, inverter, motor, regenerative braking, charging levels, and why high voltage is for trained technicians.
lessons.intro: Electric drive replaces or helps the engine with motors that run on a high-voltage battery. Fewer moving parts and no oil changes make an electric car simpler to maintain, but its high-voltage system is one area where only trained technicians belong.

blocks.html:
• Hybrid (HEV): an engine plus one or more electric motors and a battery. It can’t plug in; it charges its battery with the engine and by regenerative braking. Mild hybrids help the engine and can shut it off at stops but can’t drive on electricity alone; full hybrids can drive short distances at low speed on electricity. In the most common design, a parallel hybrid, both the engine and the motor can turn the wheels.
  • Plug-in hybrid (PHEV): a bigger battery you can charge from the grid, plus an engine for longer trips.
  • All-electric (BEV): no engine at all; a large traction battery and one or more motors. No tailpipe, no fuel pump, no fuel tank.

The traction battery stores the energy. The power electronics controller manages the flow of energy from the battery and controls the motor’s speed and torque. The traction motor turns the wheels through a transmission. The onboard charger turns AC from a wall outlet into DC for the battery, and a DC/DC converter steps the high voltage down to run the accessories and recharge a separate 12-volt battery. A thermal system keeps the battery, motor and electronics in their working temperature range.

blocks.html: Electric cars use lithium-ion cells. One cell makes about 3.7 volts, so a pack links many cells in series to reach a high voltage; high-voltage systems in electric vehicles typically range from 400 to 1,000 volts. Many manufacturers warranty their EV batteries for 8 years or 100,000 miles, and the Department of Energy expects batteries to last 12 to 15 years under normal conditions in moderate climates.

A motor becomes a generator when its shaft is turned. When you lift off the accelerator or press the brake, the car can use its motor that way, turning the wheels’ motion back into electricity for the battery instead of heat in the brakes. That recovered energy is a big part of why electric cars are so efficient: in combined driving, about 87 to 91 percent of the energy from the grid reaches the wheels, counting about 22 percent won back by regenerative braking. Brake wear drops a lot, too.
Charging speed is usually described as miles of range added per hour.

blocks.html: All-electric cars need less maintenance: fewer moving parts, and fewer fluids such as engine oil to change. Hybrids and plug-in hybrids still have engines, so their upkeep is much like a regular car’s. Tires, brakes, wipers, cabin filters and the 12-volt battery still need attention on every car (Lesson 14). One difference: the high-voltage battery can’t be jump-started. Your owner’s manual explains what to do if the car won’t power on.

blocks.h: High voltage is for trained technicians only
blocks.html:
The high-voltage battery, its orange cables and everything connected to them can carry enough energy to kill. NHTSA’s advice is plain: never try to service the traction battery without proper training and specialized equipment, and always assume the high-voltage battery and its components are energized and fully charged. Don’t touch exposed electrical parts or damaged high-voltage components.

  • After a crash, a flood or other damage, contact your dealer. Don’t store a badly damaged EV inside a building or within 50 feet of one; batteries can release flammable gases and catch fire later.
  • If you see smoke, sparks or flames, or hear gurgling or bubbling from the battery, get away from the car and call 911.

lessons.title: Thrusters and Fans on the 2026 Roadster
lessons.short: Tesla’s 2026 Roadster: cold-gas thrusters and suction fans, from Newton’s third law to choked flow and downforce, with two simulators.
lessons.intro: Tesla’s new Roadster adds two things no road car has had: thrusters that push it with jets of compressed air, and fans that suck it onto the road. Here’s what was announced, what Tesla’s patent covers, and the physics of how both work, with simulators you can run yourself.

blocks.html:
On the evening of October 15, 2026, Tesla showed its new Roadster in a livestream. It’s an electric sports car with two extras no road car has had before: cold-gas thrusters that push the car with jets of compressed air, and fans that suck the car down onto the road. Elon Musk said production should start in 2028. Tesla gave no prices. Reservations were $50,000 for the Performance version and $250,000 for the Thrust version, The Next Web reported.

Reporters watching the demonstration saw the car drive up a curved ramp and stay on it upside down, held by its fans. Thrusters then launched it off the ramp, flipped it and landed it. In another run it jumped over a row of Tesla vehicles. Tesla also showed a recorded run from 0 to 60 mph in 0.81 seconds. No one outside Tesla has checked that time yet.

Almost everything we know comes from Tesla or from reporters who watched, a day after the event. The table labels who said what. Treat the numbers as claims until independent testers measure them.

blocks.h: The patent covers the fans, not the thrusters
blocks.html:
Many people remember that Tesla filed a patent for this car. It did, but for the fans, not the thrusters. U.S. Patent 12,377,920, “Adaptive vehicle aerodynamics for downforce,” was filed on April 29, 2025, and granted to Tesla on August 5, 2025. It describes fans in air passages that pull air out of a space under the car, with skirts that reach down to the ground to close that space off. Lower pressure underneath means the air above presses the car down harder.

The patent describes two modes. In one, every skirt is down and the central fans run, for the most downforce on smooth surfaces. In the other, mainly the side skirts are down and all the fans run, for rougher ground. Its example has four fans. It gives no pressures or forces, and it never mentions thrusters, compressed gas or flight; Electrek pointed that out when the patent appeared in August 2025.

We looked for a Tesla patent on the thrusters and didn’t find one in published patent records as of October 16, 2026.

Underneath, the Roadster is an electric car: a battery pack, motors and tires, like the ones in Lesson 11. On top of that come the tanks, valves, thrusters, fans and skirts. Switch the map to Roadster (2026) to see them. Tesla hasn’t published a parts layout, so where they sit in our drawing is a sketch.

blocks.h: Push gas back, and the car goes forward
blocks.html:
A cold-gas thruster is a bottle of squeezed gas with a valve and a nozzle. Open the valve and gas rushes out of the nozzle. To throw that gas backward, the thruster has to push on it. Newton’s third law says the gas pushes back on the thruster just as hard, the other way. That push on the thruster, and so on the car, is the thrust. The Third Law chapter in the Science Lab lets you try the same idea with two skaters.

Momentum is mass times velocity. Each second the nozzle gives a mass ṁ (“m-dot”) of gas a speed ve backward, so the gas gains ṁ·ve of backward momentum every second, and the car gains the same amount forward. Force is the rate at which momentum changes, so the thrust is ṁ·ve. If the gas still has extra pressure when it leaves, that pressure pushes too and adds a second term. NASA writes the rocket thrust equation like this:
F = ṁ·v<sub>e</sub> + (p<sub>e</sub> − p<sub>a</sub>)·A<sub>e</sub>    thrust = mass flow × exit speed + (exit pressure − outside pressure) × exit area

Push for a while and you give the car an impulse: the force added up over time, J = ∫F dt. Impulse equals the change in momentum, so a thruster that pushes hard for a short time can do the same job as a weaker one that pushes longer. The Momentum and Collisions chapter shows impulse with eggs and pillows.

The jet doesn’t push on the air behind the car or on the road. It pushes only on the gas it throws out. That’s why rockets work in the vacuum of space, and it’s the idea behind the Rocket Builder. One difference: a rocket carries a huge share of its weight as fuel, while the Roadster’s air is a small share of the car, so the rocket equation’s big mass change matters much less here.

blocks.h: How much air fits in the tanks
blocks.html:
Gas pressure is the push of countless molecules hitting a wall. Squeeze more of them into the same space and they hit more often, so the pressure rises. For most gases in ordinary conditions, the ideal gas law ties it together: p·V = m·R·T. Here R is a constant for each gas (about 287 joules per kilogram per kelvin for air) and T is the temperature in kelvins. Gas in a Box lets you watch it happen with bouncing molecules.

Tesla hasn’t said how hard its tanks are pressurized. The table shows what 600 liters would hold at a few pressures. One bar is about the air pressure at sea level (one atmosphere is 1.013 bar).

blocks.html: At hundreds of bar, real air is harder to squeeze than the ideal gas law says, so a real tank holds a few to tens of percent less than these estimates. The gap grows with pressure. Even so, that’s a lot of air: at 300 bar, more than 200 kilograms. It gets used up as the thrusters fire, so the car gets a little lighter during a burn. The simulator counts that.

blocks.h: The nozzle: a speed limit at the throat
blocks.html: A thruster’s nozzle narrows to a throat, then widens into a bell. Gas speeds up as it squeezes through the narrowing. When the tank pressure is more than about 1.9 times the outside pressure (for air), the gas reaches the speed of sound right at the throat and can’t go any faster there. That’s called choked flow. Raising the tank pressure then doesn’t make the gas at the throat faster; it makes it denser, so more kilograms pass each second. NASA gives the choked mass flow as:
ṁ = A<sub>*</sub>·p<sub>t</sub>·√(γ ⁄ (R·T<sub>t</sub>))·(2 ⁄ (γ+1))<sup>(γ+1)/(2(γ−1))</sup>  ≈  0.0404·A<sub>*</sub>·p<sub>t</sub> ⁄ √T<sub>t</sub> for air, in SI units

Here A* is the throat area, pt and Tt are the pressure and temperature in the tank, and γ (gamma) is 1.4 for air and nitrogen. Past the throat, the widening bell lets the gas keep expanding and speed up beyond the speed of sound. If the bell is just the right size, the gas leaves at the outside pressure, the pressure term in the thrust equation drops out, and the exit speed is:
v<sub>e</sub> = √( 2γ⁄(γ−1) · R·T<sub>t</sub> · [1 − (p<sub>a</sub> ⁄ p<sub>t</sub>)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>] )

blocks.html:
For air at 300 bar and 20 °C, that formula gives about 690 meters per second, roughly twice the speed of sound in room air. A plain hole with no bell lets the gas out at the speed of sound (about 310 m/s for the gas, which has cooled to about −29 °C at the throat) with pressure left over. That makes less thrust for the same flow, and you can compare the two in the simulator.

NASA lists cold-gas thrusters on small spacecraft at a specific impulse of 40 to 110 seconds. Specific impulse is the effective exhaust speed divided by g, so that’s about 400 to 1,100 m/s, and our estimate sits inside that range.

“Cold gas” means nothing burns. A rocket engine burns fuel to make hot, fast gas. A cold-gas thruster only lets stored gas out. NASA describes cold-gas systems as simple and mature, with no combustion, and says most use inert, non-toxic gases such as nitrogen. The trade-off is a small total push for their size.

The gas does get cold, though, and that’s the first law of thermodynamics. The Science Lab’s Energy and the First Law chapter writes it as ΔU = Q − W: the change in a gas’s internal energy equals the heat added to it minus the work it does. When gas expands quickly, in the nozzle or in the emptying tank, there’s little time for heat to flow in, so Q is close to zero. The gas does work as it expands, so W is positive and ΔU is negative. For an ideal gas, less internal energy means a lower temperature. OpenStax puts it simply: in an adiabatic expansion, the gas does work and its temperature drops.
T<sub>2</sub> ⁄ T<sub>1</sub> = (p<sub>2</sub> ⁄ p<sub>1</sub>)<sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>    adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas (γ = 1.4 for air)

The numbers get extreme. In the ideal model, air expanding from 300 bar and 20 °C all the way down to 1 bar would cool to about −215 °C. That’s colder than −196 °C, where nitrogen boils, so real air would start to turn liquid before it got there, and any water vapor in it turns to frost long before that. The gas left in the tank cools too as its pressure falls. In the simulator, a one-second burn from 300 bar takes the tank gas from 20 °C to about −9 °C.

In physics terms, yes: it moves by throwing mass backward, like a rocket. But nothing burns. There are no flames and no hot exhaust, and the “fuel” is air that can be pumped back in; Tesla says the tanks can be refilled. That’s why it’s called a cold-gas thruster.

Choose a mode and press Fire. Boost points the thrusters backward, Brake points them forward, and Hop points them at the ground. Watch the tank pressure and temperature fall as the gas runs out, and compare the thrust with the tires’ grip and with the car’s weight. Tesla hasn’t published the tank pressure, nozzle size or the car’s weight, so those start at our guesses: 300 bar, 16 mm nozzle throats and 1,900 kg.

blocks.cap: An ideal-gas model of the thrusters, from the NASA and OpenStax equations above. It isn’t Tesla’s design: every number Tesla hasn’t published is a slider, and the notes under the graphs list the assumptions.

blocks.html: An ordinary car speeds up, brakes and turns only by pushing on the road through its tires. Friction caps that push. The most a tire can push is about μ times the force pressing it onto the road, where μ (mu) is the coefficient of friction. On flat ground that force is the car’s weight, m·g, so:
F<sub>max</sub> = μ·m·g    so the best acceleration on tires alone is a = μ·g

OpenStax lists μ = 1.0 for rubber on dry concrete and 0.7 on wet concrete. With μ = 1, no motor can get a car from 0 to 60 mph on flat ground in less than about 2.7 seconds: 60 mph is 26.8 m/s, and 26.8 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 2.7. Grip is the limit, not power. Real tires and roads vary, which is why μ is a slider. Lesson 10 covers what tires do.

Thrust doesn’t go through the tires, so friction doesn’t cap it. The thrusters push on the car directly, and the tires can still push at their limit on top of that. Tesla says its thrusters make four to five times the force the tires can handle. If Tesla’s recorded 0.81-second run is right, the car averaged 26.8 ÷ 0.81 ≈ 33 m/s² of acceleration. That’s about 3.4 g, far more than the 1 g that a grip of μ = 1 allows.

blocks.h: Fans that pull the car down
blocks.html: Air at sea level presses on everything with about 101,000 pascals, which is 101,000 newtons on every square meter. We don’t notice because it pushes equally from all sides. The fans change that. They pull air out from under the car, and the skirts slow outside air from leaking back in, so the pressure under the floor drops a little. Now the air on top pushes down harder than the air underneath pushes up. The difference is downforce:
downforce = Δp × A    pressure difference × sealed floor area

blocks.h: How little it takes to hang upside down
blocks.html:
Say the sealed area is 4 square meters and the car has a mass of 1,900 kg. Both are our guesses; Tesla hasn’t published either. The car’s weight is 1,900 × 9.8 ≈ 18,600 newtons. To hang from a ceiling, the downforce must beat that, so the pressure drop must be at least 18,600 ÷ 4 ≈ 4,700 pascals. That’s under 5% of the air’s pressure: a small drop over a big area. Driving upside down takes more, because the tires also need something to grip with.

Downforce also raises the grip limit on an ordinary road. Friction depends on how hard the tires are pressed down, so the most grip becomes μ·(m·g + downforce) while the mass the tires must move stays the same. A wing makes downforce too, but its force grows with the square of the speed and is close to zero when the car is slow. Fans make suction even when the car is parked, which is how Tesla says the Roadster can hold itself upside down while stopped.

blocks.cap: Set the pressure drop, the sealed area and the car’s mass, then flip the car to see when it can hang from a ceiling. Tesla hasn’t published any of these numbers.

blocks.html:
Compressed air stores energy, but not much for its weight. The most work a tank of gas could ever do, if it expanded slowly enough to stay at room temperature, is p·V·ln(p ⁄ pa) − (p − pa)·V. For 600 liters at 300 bar that’s about 84 megajoules, or 23 kilowatt-hours, and a fast burst gets less, because the gas cools as it expands. Per kilogram of air, the best case is about 110 watt-hours, before counting the tanks. In 2020 the Department of Energy put electric-car battery cells at about 220 watt-hours per kilogram.

Most of what the air does deliver goes into the exhaust, not the car. The gas and the car get equal and opposite momentum, but kinetic energy is ½·m·v², and the exhaust moves far faster than the car, so it carries most of the energy away. That’s why the Roadster drives on its battery and motors and saves the thrusters for bursts. Tesla says more gas means more “flight time.” It hasn’t said how long that is.

• The tank pressure, the gas, the thrust of each thruster, and how long they can fire. Tesla hasn’t published them.
  • The car’s weight, and how much the tanks and the air add to it.
  • Whether the 0.81-second run and the other times hold up in independent tests.
  • How the thrusters are controlled to flip the car and land it, and how the fan modes are used on the road.
  • Whether Tesla has applied for a patent on the thrusters. The patent we found covers the fans.
  • Which versions will be sold where. Tesla’s page says the Rocket version isn’t approved for public roads.

When Tesla or independent testers publish numbers, you can put them into the simulators above. Until then, any figure that isn’t in Tesla’s own statements is an estimate. Check what it assumes.

quiz.q: What pushes a cold-gas thruster, and the car, forward?
opts: The gas it throws backward pushes back on it
The jet pushing on the air behind the car
quiz.why: Newton’s third law: the thruster pushes the gas backward, so the gas pushes the thruster forward. Nothing burns, and the jet doesn’t need anything behind it to push on.

quiz.q: On flat ground with tire grip μ = 1, what is the best acceleration from the tires alone?
opts: As much as the motor can give
It depends only on tire width
quiz.why: Friction caps the push at μ·m·g, so the acceleration can’t beat μ·g, about 9.8 m/s² when μ = 1, however strong the motor is.

quiz.q: Why does air get colder as it rushes out of a nozzle?
opts: It does work as it expands and has no time to take in heat
quiz.why: With Q close to zero, ΔU = Q − W is negative when the gas does work. For an ideal gas, less internal energy means a lower temperature.

quiz.q: What does Tesla’s published patent US 12,377,920 describe?
opts: A way for the car to fly
Fans and skirts that lower the air pressure under the car
quiz.why: The patent, “Adaptive vehicle aerodynamics for downforce,” covers fans and skirts. It never mentions thrusters or flight.

quiz.q: A 1,900 kg car has 4 m² of sealed floor. About how big a pressure drop lets it hang from a ceiling?
opts: No pressure drop can do it
quiz.why: Its weight is about 18,600 N, and 18,600 N ÷ 4 m² ≈ 4,700 Pa, under 5% of the 101,000 Pa the air pushes with.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting by Symptom
lessons.short: An interactive finder: pick a symptom, answer a question or two, and get likely causes, safe checks and when to stop.
lessons.intro: Good troubleshooting starts with noticing. What do you see, hear, smell and feel, and when does it happen? Those clues point to a system, and the system points to a fix. This finder walks you through the common ones.

blocks.html:
1. Notice the details. When does it happen: cold or warm, at a certain speed, when braking, when turning? Does it change with engine speed or with road speed?
  2. Use your senses. Look for drips and smoke, listen for sounds, notice smells, feel for vibration and pulling.
  3. Check the simple things first. Fuel in the tank, tire pressure, fluid levels, a tight gas cap, a blown fuse.
  4. Read the codes and the warning lights. They’re clues, not answers (Lesson 5, and Read Dashboard Warning Lights).
  5. Know when to stop. Some symptoms mean pull over now. The finder marks them.

blocks.cap: Causes are listed roughly from the most common and simplest to check, to the less common. Your owner’s manual and a qualified technician have the final word for your car.

blocks.html:
• Check for open safety recalls: enter the 17-character VIN, found on the lower left of the windshield, at NHTSA’s recall site. Recall repairs are free at a dealer.

lessons.title: Doing Your Own Work
lessons.short: A basic tool kit, garage safety, and a skill ladder from first jobs to the jobs to leave to professionals.
lessons.intro: Doing your own car work saves money and teaches you how your car is put together. Start with simple checks, build skill one rung at a time, and know which jobs belong to trained professionals.

blocks.html:
You don’t need a full shop to start. This kit covers the first two rungs of the ladder below:

  • Your owner’s manual, and later the service information for your car
  • Safety glasses and nitrile or mechanic’s gloves
  • A tire pressure gauge (keep it in the car) and a tread depth gauge
  • A flashlight or headlamp, clean rags, a funnel and a drain pan
  • A socket set and wrenches in the sizes your car uses, screwdrivers and pliers
  • A torque wrench, for lug nuts and other bolts with a specified tightness
  • A jack, jack stands rated for your car’s weight, and wheel chocks
  • A digital multimeter and an OBD-II scan tool

• Exhaust: never run a car or truck inside a garage attached to a house, even with the door open; carbon monoxide is odorless and colorless and kills without warning. In a detached garage, open the door to let fresh air in before running the engine.
  • Lifting: a jack is for lifting, not holding. Before any part of you goes under the car, set it on jack stands at the lift points your owner’s manual shows, on firm, level ground. OSHA’s workplace rule puts it simply: once a load is raised, it must be blocked or otherwise secured at once.
  • Eyes: wear safety glasses around batteries, fluids, and anything under the car.
  • Batteries: keep sparks and flames away; charging batteries give off hydrogen, which can explode. Battery acid is caustic.
  • Heat: engines, exhaust parts and coolant stay hot long after you park. Never open the radiator cap on a hot engine.
  • Brake dust: no compressed air, no dry brushing; use EPA’s wet-wipe method.
  • Fluids: antifreeze is sweet-tasting and poisonous; keep it closed and away from children. Take used oil to a collection site; never pour it on the ground.

Check NHTSA’s recall site with your VIN before you buy parts; a recall repair is free. And when a job turns out bigger than you expected, it’s fine to stop and take the car to a shop.
