lessons.title: Careers in Auto Repair
lessons.short: What automotive service technicians do, how they train, what they earn, the job outlook, and ASE certification.
lessons.intro: If this course hooked you, there’s a career in it. Automotive service technicians and mechanics inspect, maintain and repair cars and light trucks, and the work keeps changing as cars add computers, sensors and electric drive.

blocks.html:
• Find problems, often with computerized diagnostic equipment
  • Test parts and systems to make sure they work properly
  • Do basic care such as oil changes, fluid checks and tire rotations
  • Repair or replace worn parts, such as brake pads, wheel bearings and sensors
  • Make repairs to manufacturer and customer specifications, and document the work
  • Explain problems and repairs to customers

The job takes problem-solving, attention to detail, steady hands, mechanical skill, some physical strength (tires and parts are heavy), and good communication with customers.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Occupational Outlook Handbook (page updated August 27, 2026), the median pay for automotive service technicians and mechanics was $50,620 a year, or $24.34 an hour, in May 2025. The lowest-paid 10 percent earned less than $34,660 and the highest-paid 10 percent more than $81,790. Pay depends on where you work: the median at automobile dealers was $59,920. Some shops pay by the hour; others pay by the amount of work completed.

There were 825,800 of these jobs in 2025, and employment is projected to grow 5 percent from 2025 to 2035, faster than the average for all occupations, with about 66,200 openings a year, mostly to replace workers who move to other jobs or retire. BLS points to more vehicles on the road, owners keeping vehicles longer, and growing demand for calibrating and repairing advanced safety systems. These figures are updated every year; check the handbook for the latest.

blocks.html:
• High school: classes in automotive repair, electronics, computers and math help. Some high schools have full automotive programs.
  • Postsecondary programs: community colleges and technical institutes offer automotive service programs, with classroom instruction and hands-on practice, that lead to a certificate or an associate’s degree. BLS lists a postsecondary nondegree award as the typical entry-level education.
  • Manufacturer or dealer programs: some programs are sponsored by automakers or dealers and focus on one make of vehicle.
  • Apprenticeships: paid on-the-job training combined with technical instruction. Registered apprenticeships let you earn a wage from day one and finish with a nationally recognized credential.
  • On the job: some start as trainee technicians, technicians’ helpers or lubrication workers and learn as they go; that path usually takes longer.

Technicians who buy or work with refrigerants must be certified by the EPA in proper refrigerant handling.

blocks.html:
The National Institute for Automotive Service Excellence (ASE) certifies technicians. To become ASE certified, you pass an ASE test and have full-time, hands-on work experience: one, two or three years for repair technicians, depending on the test. Relevant formal training can count toward part of that. Certifications are valid for five years; then you take a recertification test.

The car and light truck tests are A1 Engine Repair, A2 Automatic Transmission/Transaxle, A3 Manual Drive Train and Axles, A4 Suspension and Steering, A5 Brakes, A6 Electrical/Electronic Systems, A7 Heating and Air Conditioning, A8 Engine Performance, and A9 Light Vehicle Diesel Engines. Certification in A1 through A8 earns the title ASE-Certified Master Automobile Technician.

Students can start earlier: ASE’s Entry-Level certification is meant for students, has no work-experience requirement, and expires after two years.

The same skills lead to diesel service technicians, who work on trucks and buses, and to automotive body and glass repairers. Both have their own pages in the Occupational Outlook Handbook. More trades are listed on The Trades page.

finder.name: Won’t start
finder.q: What happens when you turn the key or press start?

opts.label: Nothing at all, or the dash lights are dim or dead
causes: A dead or weak battery
Loose or corroded battery cables or ground connections
On an automatic, the shifter not fully in Park or Neutral (a safety switch blocks the starter)
A blown fuse or an ignition switch problem
checks: Look at the dash lights and headlights: dim or dead points to the battery.
Look for loose or crusty (corroded) battery terminals; wear eye protection.
Measure battery voltage: a well-charged battery reads a bit over 12 volts; around 11.5 volts is low.
Try a jump-start if you know how (Being an Adult 101 has a guide).
opts.stop: Don’t keep cranking a dead battery. If a jump-start doesn’t work, have it checked.
opts.pro: If the battery is good and the car still won’t do anything, the problem is in the starting circuit; a technician can test it.

opts.label: A click, or rapid clicking, but the engine doesn’t turn
causes: A weak battery that can work the solenoid but not the starter
Loose or corroded battery connections
A failing starter or starter solenoid
checks: Check and clean the battery connections (eyes protected, engine off).
Measure battery voltage.
A jump-start that cranks the engine points to the battery or its connections.
opts.stop: Don’t crank for more than 30 seconds at a time; the starter can be damaged.
opts.pro: A good battery with a click and no crank usually means the starter or its wiring.

opts.label: It cranks normally but won’t start
causes: Out of fuel
A flooded engine (smell of gasoline after trying to start)
A fuel pump, ignition or sensor problem
checks: Check the fuel gauge.
Look for a check engine light; a scan tool can read stored codes.
opts.stop: If you smell strong raw fuel or see fuel dripping, stop trying and have it checked.
opts.pro: No spark or no fuel takes testing equipment to pin down.

opts.label: Gauge in the red, warning light, or steam from under the hood
causes: Low coolant from a leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
A cooling fan that isn’t running
A thermostat stuck closed
A failed water pump or a broken belt
checks: Pull over as soon as it’s safe and turn the engine off.
Let it cool. Never open the radiator cap or pressurized system while it’s hot.
When cool, check the coolant level in the reservoir and look for leaks (green, blue or orange drips; sweet smell).
opts.stop: Stop driving as soon as it’s safe. An overheating engine can be badly damaged.
opts.pro: Have the cooling system pressure-tested and the cause found before you drive again.

opts.label: It runs hot only in traffic, fine on the highway
causes: The cooling fan not switching on or running slowly
Low coolant
A radiator blocked by debris
checks: With the engine warm and idling, see whether the fan runs. Keep hands, hair and clothing clear of it.
Check the coolant level when cold.
opts.stop: If the gauge climbs toward red, pull over and let it cool.
opts.pro: Fan circuits and sensors need testing.

opts.label: It takes a long time to warm up, and the heater is weak
causes: A thermostat stuck open
Low coolant
checks: Check the coolant level when cold.
Watch whether the gauge reaches its usual spot after a normal warm-up.
opts.stop: Not urgent, but have it fixed: an engine that runs cold wastes fuel, and you need the heater to clear the windshield.
opts.pro: A technician can confirm the cause.

finder.name: Check engine light
finder.q: Is the light steady or flashing?

opts.label: Steady
causes: A loose or missing gas cap
An emission part such as an oxygen sensor or EVAP leak
A misfire, a sensor fault, or many other possibilities
checks: Make sure the gas cap is on and tight; the light may take a few days to go off.
Read the code with a scan tool (the connector is under the driver’s side of the dash).
Note how the car runs: rough, weak, or normal?
opts.stop: Not an emergency, but get it diagnosed soon. Delays can make repairs costlier.
opts.pro: A code points to a system, not a part. A technician tests before replacing.

opts.label: Flashing
causes: A severe engine misfire: a spark plug, coil, injector or compression problem
checks: Reduce speed and avoid heavy loads.
Read the code if you can (P0300 and P0301 are examples of misfire codes).
opts.stop: Get it addressed right away and drive as little as possible: a severe misfire can damage the catalytic converter.
opts.pro: Misfire diagnosis needs testing equipment.

opts.label: Red oil pressure light (oil can)
causes: Low oil level
A failing oil pump or sensor
Worn engine bearings
checks: Pull over when it’s safe and shut the engine off.
After it sits a few minutes, check the oil level.
opts.stop: Don’t keep driving with the oil pressure light on. Loss of oil pressure can ruin the engine.
opts.pro: If the oil level is fine and the light stays on, have it towed or checked before driving.

opts.label: Battery or charging light
causes: An alternator not charging
A loose or broken drive belt
Loose or corroded battery connections
checks: Turn off things you don’t need (radio, heated seats).
With a meter, a running engine should show about 13.5 to 14.5 volts at the battery.
opts.stop: The car is running on battery alone and may stall when it’s drained. Head to a safe place or a shop.
opts.pro: Charging-system testing is quick for a shop.

opts.label: Red brake light
causes: The parking brake is on
Low brake fluid (worn pads or a leak)
A problem in one of the two brake circuits
checks: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Check the brake fluid level at the reservoir.
opts.stop: If the light stays on with the parking brake off, have the brakes checked before driving.
opts.pro: Brake hydraulics are a job for a technician.

opts.label: Tire pressure (TPMS) light
causes: At least one tire significantly under-inflated
A cold morning lowering all the pressures
If it flashes for 60 to 90 seconds and then stays on, a TPMS fault
checks: Check all four tires (and the spare) with a gauge and fill to the pressure on the door label.
Look for nails or damage.
opts.stop: If a tire is flat or badly low, don’t drive on it; change it or call for help.
opts.pro: A TPMS fault or a slow leak needs a tire shop.

opts.label: ABS or airbag light
causes: A fault in the antilock brake system
A fault in the airbag system
checks: Note when it came on; a scan tool that reads those systems can read codes.
opts.stop: Drive carefully and get it checked soon: the system may not work when you need it.
opts.pro: Airbag systems are for trained technicians only. Never take apart the steering wheel or airbag parts yourself.

opts.label: Squeal that rises with engine speed
causes: A loose or worn drive belt (power steering, fan or A/C belt)
checks: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks, shine or fraying.
opts.stop: Not usually urgent, but a broken belt can stop the alternator and water pump.
opts.pro: Belt replacement is a moderate job; tension and routing matter.

opts.label: Screech or grinding when braking
causes: Brake pad wear indicators (screech)
Pads worn to metal (grinding)
checks: Look at the pads through the wheel if you can.
opts.stop: Grinding means metal on metal: have the brakes serviced before driving further.
opts.pro: Pads and rotors are replaced in pairs on an axle.

opts.label: Click that follows engine speed
causes: Low engine oil
A stuck valve lifter
A loose or bent fan blade
checks: Check the oil level.
opts.stop: If the oil is low, add the right oil before driving more.
opts.pro: Valve train noises need diagnosis.

opts.label: Ping or rattle when accelerating
causes: Fuel with lower octane than the car needs
Ignition timing or engine deposits if it continues
checks: Use the fuel grade in your owner’s manual.
opts.stop: If the right fuel doesn’t fix it, have it checked.
opts.pro: Timing and knock-sensor problems need diagnosis.

opts.label: Heavy, rhythmic knock from the engine
causes: Worn crankshaft or connecting rod bearings
A loose torque converter
checks: Check the oil level (low oil can cause bearing damage).
opts.stop: Stop driving and have it checked.
opts.pro: Have it towed for diagnosis.

opts.label: Rumble or roar from under the car
causes: A hole or leak in the exhaust pipe, converter or muffler
A worn U-joint or other driveline part
checks: With the car parked and cool, look for loose, rusted or hanging exhaust parts.
opts.stop: An exhaust leak can let carbon monoxide build up inside the car. Get it fixed promptly.
opts.pro: Exhaust and driveline repairs need a lift.

opts.label: Clunk over bumps
causes: A loose shock absorber or other suspension part
A worn ball joint or sway bar link
A loose exhaust pipe or muffler
checks: Notice whether it happens over bumps, when turning, or both.
opts.stop: If steering feels loose or the clunk gets worse, have it checked promptly.
opts.pro: Suspension parts are best inspected on a lift.

opts.label: Burned toast or burning plastic
causes: An electrical short and burning insulation
checks: Pull over, turn the car off, and look for smoke.
opts.stop: Don’t drive until it’s checked. Shorts can start fires.
opts.pro: Electrical faults need a technician.

opts.label: Rotten eggs
causes: A problem in the catalytic converter or other emission control parts
checks: Look for a check engine light.
opts.stop: Not usually urgent, but have it checked.
opts.pro: Emission repairs may be under warranty.

opts.label: Thick, acrid burning oil
causes: Oil leaking onto hot engine or exhaust parts
Oil burning in the engine
checks: Check the oil level and look for leaks.
opts.stop: If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
opts.pro: Find and fix the leak before it gets worse.

opts.label: Gasoline
causes: A flooded engine after a failed start
A fuel leak
checks: Look for drips under the car, from a distance.
opts.stop: If the smell is strong or you see fuel, don’t start the car. Fuel vapor catches fire easily.
opts.pro: Fuel system leaks are for a technician.

opts.label: Sweet and steamy
causes: A coolant leak: a hose, radiator, water pump or heater core
checks: When the engine is cold, check the coolant reservoir; look for green, blue or orange drips.
opts.stop: Watch the temperature gauge; stop if it climbs.
opts.pro: Have the cooling system pressure-tested.

finder.name: Smoke color
finder.q: What color is the exhaust smoke?

opts.label: Blue or blue-gray
causes: Oil burning in the cylinders: worn rings or valve guides
Too much oil in the crankcase, or a clogged breather
A leaking turbocharger seal
checks: Check the oil level; overfilled oil is a simple cause.
Notice whether you’re adding oil often.
opts.stop: Not usually an emergency; keep the oil topped up and have it diagnosed.
opts.pro: Engine wear needs testing (compression or leak-down).

opts.label: Black
causes: Too much fuel or too little air: a clogged air filter, injector or sensor trouble
checks: Check the engine air filter.
Look for a check engine light.
opts.stop: Have it checked; it wastes fuel and power.
opts.pro: Fuel control problems need diagnosis.

opts.label: White
causes: Thin white vapor on a cold start that goes away: normal condensation
Thick white smoke that keeps coming after warm-up: possibly coolant getting into the cylinders
checks: Watch whether it clears as the engine warms.
When cold, check whether the coolant level is dropping.
opts.stop: If white smoke continues and coolant is disappearing, stop driving and have it checked.
opts.pro: A cooling-system pressure test can find internal leaks.

opts.label: Yellowish green, pastel blue or bright orange
causes: Coolant (antifreeze): a hose, water pump or radiator
checks: Check the coolant reservoir when cold.
Clean it up: antifreeze is poisonous and tastes sweet to children and pets.
opts.stop: Watch the temperature gauge; stop if it climbs.
opts.pro: Have the leak found and fixed.

opts.label: Dark brown or black, oily
causes: Engine oil from a bad seal or gasket
checks: Check the oil level and keep it topped up.
opts.stop: A big puddle means check the level before driving.
opts.pro: Have the source found.

opts.label: Red, oily
causes: Transmission fluid
Power-steering fluid
checks: Note where it drips: under the middle or front of the car.
opts.stop: Low transmission fluid can damage the transmission; get it checked soon.
opts.pro: Fluid checks and repairs vary by car.

opts.label: Clear water
causes: Usually condensation from the air conditioner: normal
checks: Feel it: plain water isn’t oily or slippery.
opts.stop: No action needed for plain water.
opts.pro: If it’s oily or slippery, or drips near a wheel, have it identified before driving; it could be from the brakes.

opts.label: At certain speeds, through the steering wheel or seat
causes: A wheel out of balance
A bent wheel or damaged tire
A driveshaft or U-joint problem
checks: Look at the tires for bulges, uneven wear or missing balance weights.
opts.stop: If the vibration is new and strong, slow down and have it checked.
opts.pro: Balancing needs a tire shop’s machine.

opts.label: Only when braking
causes: Uneven or damaged brake rotors
checks: Notice whether you feel it in the pedal, the steering wheel, or both.
opts.stop: Have the brakes checked soon.
opts.pro: Rotors may need resurfacing or replacing.

opts.label: At idle or when the engine runs rough
causes: A misfire
checks: Look for a check engine light and read the code.
opts.stop: If the check engine light flashes, follow the flashing-light advice.
opts.pro: Misfires need diagnosis.

opts.label: While driving straight
causes: An under-inflated tire
Alignment out (camber or caster uneven)
Damaged or worn steering or suspension parts
checks: Check all tire pressures with a gauge.
Look for uneven tire wear.
opts.stop: If the pull is sudden or strong, slow down and check the tires.
opts.pro: Alignment takes special equipment and a qualified technician.

opts.label: Only when braking
causes: A brake problem on one side, such as a sticking caliper
An under-inflated tire
checks: Check the tire pressures.
opts.stop: Have the brakes checked before driving more than you must.
opts.pro: Brake diagnosis is a job for a technician.

opts.label: Spongy or springy
causes: Air in the brake lines
Old fluid that has absorbed water
checks: Check the brake fluid level.
opts.stop: Don’t drive until the brakes are checked.
opts.pro: Bleeding the brakes needs the right procedure for your car.

opts.label: Sinks slowly toward the floor when held
causes: A leak inside the master cylinder
An outside fluid leak
checks: Look for wet spots near the wheels and under the master cylinder.
opts.stop: Don’t drive. Have it towed or checked where it sits.
opts.pro: Master cylinder and line repairs are for a technician.

opts.label: Very hard to push
causes: A failed power brake booster or vacuum leak
A collapsed hose or binding linkage
checks: Listen for a hiss when you press the pedal.
opts.stop: Have it checked before driving; stopping takes far more effort.
opts.pro: Booster diagnosis is a shop job.

opts.label: Pulses, or grinds
causes: ABS working on a slippery road: it releases and reapplies the brakes rapidly, which you can feel
Uneven rotors
Pads worn to metal (grinding)
checks: Note whether it happens only on slippery roads.
opts.stop: Grinding means stop and have the brakes serviced.
opts.pro: Rotors and pads are replaced in pairs.
